title: Bhuman — the infinite, where one sees nothing else (7.23–7.24)
hook: at the top of the ladder Sanatkumara says it plainly: there's no happiness in the small; the infinite is happiness
tomorrow: the city of Brahman in the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday: meditation, understanding, strength, food, water, the ladder asking what holds each thing up. Your line was the ladder climbs. What did you trace down to its support? Day three hundred fifty-five.

Think of the happiest you've been that you didn't notice at the time. Maybe it was swimming in the ocean as a kid. Maybe it was a late night laughing with friends until it hurt. Maybe a concert, or holding a newborn. Here's the odd thing about those moments: you weren't thinking, I'm happy. You weren't thinking anything. There was no you over here and the happiness over there. There was just it. Sanatkumara's ladder, after many rungs, arrives at exactly that.
screen: `HAPPY, AND DIDN'T NOTICE.` → `NO YOU OVER HERE.` → `JUST IT.`

segments.voice: Between yesterday and today, the ladder climbs through heat, space, memory, hope, and breath, and then turns toward truth, understanding, faith and action. And at the top Sanatkumara says: a person acts only when they find happiness. So, Narada, you should want to understand happiness. Then the line this chapter is known for. Yo vai bhuma tat sukham, nalpe sukham asti. The infinite is happiness. There is no happiness in the small. Bhuma means the vast, the full, the unbounded. Alpa means the small, the limited. And here's how you tell them apart: where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else, that is the infinite. Where one sees something else, hears something else, understands something else, that is the small. Think back to the ocean, the laughter, the newborn. Nothing else, for a moment. That's a taste of what he means. Narada asks a reasonable question: but sir, what does the infinite rest on? And Sanatkumara answers: on its own greatness. Or, not even on greatness. Then he explains what he doesn't mean. People here call cows and horses greatness, he says, and elephants and gold, servants and spouses, fields and houses. I don't mean that. Those things rest on something else. The infinite doesn't rest on anything. It's above and below, east and west, everywhere. And then he says: I am all this. The self is all this. The chapter ends quietly, saying Sanatkumara showed Narada the far shore beyond darkness.
screen: `WE ACT TO FIND HAPPINESS.` · `NO HAPPINESS IN THE SMALL.` · `WHERE ONE SEES NOTHING ELSE.` · `NOT COWS, GOLD OR HOUSES.` · then, large: `YO VAI BHUMA TAT SUKHAM.`

segments.voice: Today's practice rests in the wide. Sit and settle. Let your attention spread out: the sounds in the room, then beyond the room, then as far as you can hear. Let your sense of space open: above you, below you, on every side. Don't hold on to any one thing. When a thought pulls you into something small, notice it, and let the space open again. Just wide, and breathing. The bell holds the time.
Bhuman. The infinite, the vast: where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else. There's no happiness in the small.
Your line: the infinite is happiness. Today, notice one moment when you get so absorbed that there's nothing else, and let it be enough. Day three hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote 'the infinite is happiness; there is no happiness in the small' when distinguishing lasting joy from pleasure in possessions, and the bhuma-vidya is a standard topic in Vedanta study.

match.prompt: the infinite and the small — tap the pairs.

myth: Sanatkumara says cows, gold and houses are true greatness
people call that greatness. he says he doesn't mean that.
the infinite rests on its own greatness, or not even on that
everything else rests on something else.
the chapter ends with Narada still in sorrow
it says Sanatkumara showed him the far shore beyond darkness.

fork.setup: you're Narada. Sanatkumara has said the infinite is happiness. you ask what the infinite rests on. what does he answer?
options: on its own greatness, or not even on greatness.
on cows, gold and good houses.
fork.reveal: it rests on nothing else. the things people call greatness rest on something; the infinite is everywhere.

original.note: Sanskrit bhūmā (stem bhūman): the vast, the infinite, fullness. yo vai bhūmā tat sukham.

trapdoor: what you thought: think big, be happy.
what it means: lasting happiness is the infinite, where there's nothing else; anything with an outside is small and passes.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 7.23–7.24, the bhuma-vidya; the Brahma Sutras (1.3.8) discuss whether bhuma here means prana or Brahman.
